# On the Peculiar Joy of Getting Lost

There's something I've been thinking about lately—something that catches me off guard every time it happens, which is more often than you'd think. It's that moment when you realize you have absolutely no idea where you are, and instead of panic, something closer to delight floods through you.

I don't mean the dangerous kind of lost, the kind that ends with a frantic call to roadside assistance or your spouse giving you that particular look of resignation. I mean the gentle lost, the kind where you took a turn you weren't sure about, and now you're on a street you've never seen before, and your phone's battery is low enough that you're conserving it like it's a precious resource, and somehow that constraint feels liberating rather than limiting.

This happens to me most when I'm walking. There's something about walking that makes getting lost feel like discovery instead of failure. A car zooms you past everything in your rush to reach a predetermined destination. But walking—walking lets you notice. You notice the way light falls through an awning. You notice the smell of someone's dinner through an open window. You notice that there's a bookstore you never knew existed, or a park bench facing something worth facing, or that an alley has been transformed into a small garden by someone with more time or hope or both than most people seem to have.

I think we're supposed to feel ashamed of being lost. Our culture has built this entire infrastructure—maps, GPS, street signs, appointment apps—around the premise that we should always know where we are and where we're going. Uncertainty is inefficiency. Wandering is wasting time. The shortest distance between two points is a straight line, and we've become so obsessed with that line that we've forgotten to look at what exists just beyond it.

But there's a kind of wisdom in the lost moment, or maybe it's just honesty. When you're genuinely lost, you can't pretend to be somewhere you're not. You can't be going somewhere with purpose when you don't actually know the way. There's a vulnerability in it that's oddly clarifying. You have to admit: I don't know. I was wrong. I need to figure something out. These are not statements we make easily in normal life.

The pandemic did something to me—I suspect it did something to most of us—that made the idea of purposefulness feel more fragile. For months, we were all stripped of our destination. There was nowhere to go, nothing to do, no trajectory to maintain. It was terrible and strange and sometimes surprisingly peaceful. And afterward, when we emerged and got back to the business of going places and accomplishing things, I found I couldn't quite muster the same faith in the importance of always knowing exactly where I was headed.

This doesn't mean I've become irresponsible. I still show up to things. I still honor my commitments. But I've become suspicious of the assumption that being lost is something to be corrected as quickly as possible. Sometimes the correction takes longer than the detour.

There's a particular kind of person who plans everything down to the minute. I used to be more like this than I am now. I had systems. I had backup plans for my backup plans. And yes, that meant I rarely missed anything or disappointed anyone, but it also meant I was living according to a script I'd written in advance, and I missed the chance to be surprised by anything, including myself.

The novelist Anne Lamott has this concept about "shitty first drafts." The idea is that you have to write badly first to write well eventually. You have to be willing to make mistakes, to go places that don't end up in the final version, to waste time and energy on dead ends. The alternative is paralysis—waiting until you're perfect to begin, which means never beginning.

I think the same is true of life. We need more shitty first drafts. We need more wrong turns and strange detours and moments where we stop being the protagonist of our own movie and just become a person in the world, genuinely uncertain about what comes next.

There's also something about being lost that makes you more present. Your body is here, your attention is here, because you're actually paying attention to where you are rather than where you're supposed to be. You're looking at street names and storefronts and people. You're noticing. You're actually in your life instead of moving through it like you're driving somewhere on autopilot.

Some of my best days have happened because I was lost. A conversation with a stranger I met while asking for directions. A restaurant I found by accident and still think about years later. A street that had light in a particular way that made me understand something about beauty I hadn't grasped before. These weren't on the itinerary. They were bonuses, gifts, accidents.

I suppose what I'm really thinking about is the difference between existing and living. It's possible to exist while knowing exactly where you're going, while executing the plan, while staying on the mapped route. And it's possible to live while being utterly lost, while following a thread of curiosity into unknown streets, while being willing to not know what comes next.

Neither is wrong. We need both—we need the structure and the plans, the knowledge of where we're headed. But we also need the margin, the space off the map, the permission to be lost.

I don't know where this thought is headed, if I'm being honest. I started writing it knowing something was there but not quite what. And that's okay. That's maybe the whole point. Not everything needs a destination. Sometimes the walking is the point. Sometimes getting lost is how you find the thing you didn't know you were looking for.
